title: The Ardas's last line
hook: Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhaane sarbat da bhala: through the Name, rising spirits; by Your will, good for all

segments.voice: Yesterday: bhul chuk, and your line: forgive the errors. Today, the very last words of the Ardas.

How do you end something big? A letter ends with love. A speech ends with thank you. A phone call ends, in some families, with five rounds of okay, bye, okay, bye. Last words carry weight because they're what stays in the room. The Ardas has walked through Sikh history: the Gurus, the martyrs, the homes left behind, today's reason, an apology for any slip. Then it ends on one line, the same line every time, in gurdwaras from Amritsar to Toronto.
screen: `HOW DO YOU END SOMETHING BIG?` → `LAST WORDS STAY IN THE ROOM.` → `THE SAME LINE, EVERY TIME.`

segments.voice: Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhaane sarbat da bhala. Take it in two halves. First: Nanak naam chardi kala. Naam is the Name, the Sikh word for living in awareness of the One. Chardi kala is rising spirit: a spirit that climbs instead of sinking, hopeful and steady even in hard times. Sikhs read this half in more than one way. Some hear: Nanak, through the Name may there be rising spirits. Others hear: through the Name given by Nanak, rising spirits. Either way, the source of the uplift is the Name, not luck or mood. Second: tere bhaane sarbat da bhala. Tere bhaane, in Your will. Sarbat, everyone, all of it. Bhala, good, well-being. In Your will, may there be good for all. Look at what this does after everything before it. Moments ago the prayer was about one family's surgery or one student's exam. Now it widens all the way out. Not good for Sikhs. Not good for the people in this room. Good for all, with no one left off the list. And the order: rising spirits first, then good for everyone. A sinking spirit has a hard time wishing anyone well. A climbing one can afford to be generous. This line is recited at the close of the Ardas, not found as a verse in the Guru Granth Sahib itself; it gathers up ideas that run all through it. When it's said, the congregation bows, and the prayer is done.
screen: `NAAM: THE NAME.` · `CHARDI KALA: A RISING SPIRIT.` · `TERE BHAANE: IN YOUR WILL.` · `SARBAT DA BHALA: GOOD FOR ALL.` · then, large: `RISING SPIRITS, GOOD FOR ALL.`

segments.voice: Sit tall. On an in-breath, think chardi kala, rising spirit, and let your chest lift a little; on the out-breath, think sarbat da bhala, good for all, and let the good go out past this room, to your street, to people you'll never meet, to someone you find hard. If you pray, say the whole line softly: Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhaane sarbat da bhala.
Chardi kala, rising spirit, optimism that climbs even in hard times: through the Name, Nanak naam chardi kala; in Your will, good for all, tere bhaane sarbat da bhala.
Your line: rising spirits, good for all. The same last words, every single time. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 635 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE GURU IS THE GRANTH.`

howItsDone: Every Ardas ends with Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhaane sarbat da bhala; the congregation then bows, and many follow with the couplet about the Guru Granth and the jaikara.

what a scholar hears: the line is a liturgical close, not a scriptural verse; its first half is read either as a vocative to Nanak or as 'the Name given by Nanak', and Sikhs hold both readings.

chat.says: The Sikh prayer ends with 'sarbat da bhala.' Good for who, exactly?
options: For everyone, with no one left off the list, right after a wish for rising spirits.
For the Sikhs in the room, since the prayer was made by them and for them.
For the family whose reason was named, as the prayer's very last request.
chat.meaning: Tere bhaane sarbat da bhala: in Your will, good for all. After one household's reason, the Ardas widens out to everyone.

chardi kala.meaning: rising spirit, hopeful and steady even in hard times
